          user63 edited 2026-08-31 12:35:27

          That being said, personal computing will get much more expensive, and people will start to look for cheaper alternatives. I’m probably wrong but I think things such as electronics repairs and custom computer builds will make a resurgence.

          I think you might be onto something. The market for consumer electronics repair in particular has been hurt from two sides. The first one is that big manufacturers have been hostile to repair, which we all know and rightfully condemn.

          But the other is that for a long time, if your device failed, there would be a new one this year, often with better features, generally for the same price or less. So if some non-trivial component in your smartphone, game console, TV, etc failed, and you looked into repairing it, you'd often get the old "It would cost so much to repair this that you might as well buy a new one," which I'm sure we've all run into.

          The latter might be changing, at least for some categories of devices. The new Google Pixel 11 Pro (base model) costs more than one from the previous generation, but has less RAM -- and the same as the three year old Pixel 8 Pro I'm typing this on. I think new Samsungs are losing RAM and maybe some other features vs previous generations, too.

          It's unclear how long this will last, and as a consumer of electronics, who wants to be able to get a shiny new thing for a good price, I hope this doesnt't last. But as someone who cares about reducing e-waste, and wants to keep hardware running for as long as it can be useful, I'm almost ... hopeful that the economics around repair, warped by "it makes more sense to just buy a new one", might get unwarped.

          So in a situation where the new thing costs more than what you paid for your 3 year old thing, but is not significantly better wrt features, people might be more economically motivated to seek repair, and independent repair shops would make more sense as a business. That would be pretty rad.

            Exactly, that’s how I think, too. But… I’m aware this is a very short-term view that is highly contingent on the current circumstances (Big Tech eating the world, a global cost of living crisis affecting developed countries, etc.). Also, that’s my idea on how would I survive to it if it ever came to the point where I had to leave the software industry. There’s also a good amount of wishful thinking I left in.

            In reality, I think the best reference we might have is the automotive industry post-pandemic (I’m in Europe so that will be a biased take). After the German economy sharted itself and their auto makers botched electrification, cheap Chinese EVs started selling like hot cakes. All of that is to say, Chinese manufacturers may smell the blood in the retail computing sector and come up with something we don’t expect. There are reasons why I believe this is unlikely, one of them being that hardware is basically a commodity and the global market is more focused on software solutions that are highly dependent on, say, x86-64, which are far from being the focus of the Chinese economy at this point. But I wouldn’t rule it out.

            P.S. How I miss the times where I had such discussions with my coworkers, instead of hearing to their takes on how gen AI will eat the world and the next model with one bajillion parameters will be the nail on the coffin of programmers, etc.

                I decided to stop spending any time at all applying to job ads and spend a bunch more time just reconnecting with people, talking to them and essentially reminding them that I exist and that we used to talk. One of the leads is also in exactly the type of job that I want, working with people who are far more experienced than I (20+ years in a pretty niche area), so it's possible that I'll literally have to choose between really good money or potentially a wealth of knowledge to soak in.

                  I had a similar experience two years ago. It was maddening to be desk rejected for jobs for which, AFAICT, my resume demonstrated all the requirements.

                  As others have suggested, I think there’s an abundance of qualified people looking for relatively senior roles.                   About five years ago I was a hiring manager. Picking five folks to interview from twenty resumes is brutal. In the end, I think it was mostly random.                                     user24 edited 2026-08-30 08:27:49

                                    As a person who has been in hundreds of recruiting processes on both sides, the best advice I can give to skilled engineers is: Reject all BS immediately.

                                    It's better that both parties come to an honest conclusion early rather than later. The best jobs I had, were both sides secured the position early because both realized it was a good fit.

                                    For a competent and experiences engineer, the whole set up of acting like the company is in a position of power and you are the one begging for something, it's just absurd. Just reject that premise. If they talk to you like that, just politely state that it's not what you are looking for.

                                    I stopped accepting doing coding tests years ago. The reason being that the ones evaluating the test usually had less expertize in the subject than myself. So what was the point? Same for references, why would I bother an ex coworker for a position that the hiring party is not sure about? I am happy sending code samples or if they manage to find their own references, but the whole idea that you are begging for some privilege is just absurd.

                                    Think of it as business which is what it is. Everything else is just really used to put you in a position of disadvantage.

                                    Once the contract is sign, then sure, embrace the team, be a good worker, socialize with your coworkers, and so on. But only then. But only from the moment you signed your contract.

                                    If you do this, you protect yourself against feeling rejected. You only feel rejected because you accepted the premise that your job is a privilege. Which I supose in many cases it is. Personally I see no point into getting a job where I am easily replaceable. If the company has a stake into having you there, then they will be committed to keep you, not lay you off.
